newsitem.title: UK: European Crude Outlook - Iraq tests N.Sea nerves.
newsitem.headline: European Crude Outlook - Iraq tests N.Sea nerves.

text.p: Iraq will hold sway over North Sea crude prices this week with bears predicting a rapid resumption of Baghdad's oil exports and bulls betting on continued delays, traders said.
The fate of Baghdad's second 180-day period of exports under the U.N. "oil-for-food" programme could prolong the firmer physical market seen last week or send it crashing into reverse.
Most players agreed Iraqi news will outweigh anything OPEC, meeting in Vienna this week, is likely to decide on tackling the group's chronic overproduction.
"This market could get so soft so quickly on any bearish news out of Iraq. Take Iraq out of the equation and it's a much softer market," said one trader.
"Iraq is the story to watch. OPEC isn't going to attract that much attention," said another trader.
Ministers of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC) start arriving in Vienna on Monday for regular production talks due to start on Wednesday.
But the group is not expected to curb its output despite a 30 percent drop in the price of crude since the start of the year.

Top news from the meeting could well be word from the Iraqi delegation, led by oil minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed, about when exports are likely to resume and unleash more than 700,000 bpd into the market.
Bulls took heart last week when Iraq said it would refuse to sell more oil until $800 million of its export proceeds held in an escrow account was spent on humanitarian supplies and food.
More support came from worsening disputes between Iraq and United Nations officials dismantling Baghdad's weapons of mass desturcxtion under Gulf War resolutions.
Sellers also cite thinner than expected July North Sea loading programmes that helped lift Dated Brent over 10 cents to August Brent -45 cents and boost other grades by similar amounts.
But bears counter that worsening refinery profit margins hit by lower product prices and firmer crudes should temper demand and require sellers to lower offers.
Cracking returns for Brent in Rotterdam fell to $1.97 a barrel late last week from almost $3 the previous week.
Another key unknown remains the fate of five Brents in the hands of a European major said to be seeking to move the barrels into the U.S. Gulf.

In the Mediterranean, sour crude values remain buoyant and supply scarce in the absence of Iraqi Kirkuk. Urals has risen to around Dated Brent -95 cents from -$1.15 a week ago on tight supply and solid demand.
Syria is seeking higher prices for its crude oil in July but customers are resisting for fear a resumption of Iraqi exports would send spot prices tumbling.
State-owned Sytrol has telexed term contract holders with an opening offer of Dated Brent -55 cents a barrel for its key Syrian Light crude, an increase of 22 cents over June.
But most regular lifters of Syrian crude are seeking a rollover of June's Dated Brent -77 cents a barrel, although a modest increase would be acceptable to some.
Regional benchmark Russian Urals has seen its discount to Dated Brent slashed by 40 cents since the beginning of June amid uncertainty about Iraqi exports.
-- William Maclean London newsroom +44 171 542 7646
